opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really promising approach, and in some ways it's one of the cleaner sources of ground truth we have for training judgment, as opposed to just training a model to imitate what people wrote.

The basic appeal is this. Much of what we want from advanced AI is good forecasting and good strategic judgment: which policies will work, which research directions will pan out, how a negotiation or a war or a market will unfold. Normally that's hard to train, because the feedback comes slowly and you can't run history twice. But if you freeze a model's knowledge at, say, 2015, you have a decade of real outcomes to score it against. You can ask it thousands of questions, about elections, GDP, which startups succeed, which scientific results replicate, and grade it on reality rather than on whether a human rater liked the answer. That's an enormous, objective reward signal for exactly the kind of reasoning that's hardest to supervise directly.

It also helps with a deeper problem. If you train models only on human feedback, you risk teaching them to say what sounds persuasive to evaluators. Grading against what actually happened rewards being right, not being convincing. That matters a lot for trustworthiness. If you later want to rely on an AI's advice in high-stakes situations where humans can't easily check the reasoning, a demonstrated track record of calibrated predictions on held-out history is evidence you can actually lean on.

There are real technical challenges. The biggest is leakage: making sure information from after the cutoff hasn't crept into the training data through later edits, retrospective articles, or even subtle stylistic cues about what became important. You need careful data hygiene, and probably several staggered cutoffs so you can check whether performance holds up. There's also the question of how much history you have. The world gives you only one run, so the number of truly independent big-picture outcomes is limited, and you have to avoid overfitting to the particular path history took. Calibration across many smaller questions helps a lot with that.

Overall, I'd say it's one of the more valuable directions for building AI that's actually wise rather than just fluent. It also fits with a broader theme I care about: if AI is going to help humanity navigate an extremely consequential transition, we want systems whose forecasting and advice we have good reason to trust, and we want that capacity available early, before the most critical decisions get made. Retrodiction-style training and evaluation is a concrete, scalable way to get there.

r001.rationale: The response says that truly independent big-picture outcomes are limited, but does not identify correlations among large-scale historical events as the reason.

r002.rationale: It discusses post-cutoff information leaking into training data, but not fine-tuning on one prediction revealing answers to related questions used as held-out tests.

r003.rationale: It does not mention uncorrelated factors in individual people's outcomes as a source of long-term forecasting data.

r004.rationale: It presents historical outcomes as a reward signal for training judgment, but does not say fine-tuning helps the AI apply intelligence acquired during prior training.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a really interesting idea, and it's one that I've found appealing for a while, basically because it gives you an enormous amount of training signal that's grounded in reality rather than in human judgment.

So the way to think about it: a lot of what we want from these systems is good judgment about the world, good forecasting, the ability to reason from a body of evidence to what's actually going to happen. And ordinarily, if you want to train a model to be a good forecaster, you run into the problem that the future takes a long time to arrive. You can set up forecasting tournaments, you can have it make predictions, and then you wait months or years to score them. That's a very slow feedback loop.

But if you train a model only on data up to, say, 2015, you now have a decade of history that the model has never seen, and every event in that period is a question with a known answer. You can ask about elections, scientific discoveries, which companies succeeded, which technologies panned out, how a war played out, what a particular paper's results were going to be. And you can generate essentially unlimited numbers of these questions automatically, because the answers are just sitting there in the later corpus. That's a very attractive property compared to things like RLHF, where you're paying humans to produce labels and the labels inherit all the biases and limitations of the labelers.

There are a few things I'd flag, though.

One is the leakage problem, which is harder than it sounds. It's not enough to filter documents by their publication date. Lots of text written before the cutoff gets edited afterwards, or refers to things in ways that are only available in later versions. Wikipedia pages are the obvious case. And then there are subtler things: a document from 2014 that was selected for inclusion in a dataset in 2020 may have been selected because it turned out to be important, and that selection effect itself carries information about the future. So if you want clean evaluation, you need to be quite careful, and the model will be very good at picking up on whatever leakage exists.

A second is that the distribution of events in the period after the cutoff is one draw of history. The model is learning to predict the specific decade that actually happened, and you want it to generalise to good forecasting in general rather than overfitting to the particular contingencies of that period. I think that's manageable, because the number of distinct questions is so large and they're so varied, but it's something to watch. You'd ideally want to see that the skill transfers to genuinely held-out, post-training events.

A third is more about what this does and doesn't give you. Predicting history is a great way to sharpen a model's world model and its calibration. It's less clear that it helps with things like mathematical ability or coding, where you already have good verifiable signals from other sources. So I'd see it as complementary rather than as a replacement for other forms of training.

And then there's a point that I think matters from the safety side. A model that's been heavily optimised to predict what actually happened is being optimised to be accurate about the world, including about human behaviour, politics, how institutions respond to things. That's quite valuable for making the model useful as an advisor. But it's also, by construction, making it a better modeler of people, which cuts both ways. I don't think that's a reason not to do it, but it is one more reason to want the alignment and oversight work to keep pace with these capability-enhancing methods rather than lagging behind.

On the whole, though, I'd say I'm positive on it. If you ask what are the cheap, scalable sources of ground truth that aren't just "did the code compile" or "did a human rater like this", history is one of the biggest ones, and it's a bit surprising it hasn't been exploited more aggressively already.

r002.rationale: It discusses document leakage and selection effects, but does not explain how fine-tuning on one historical prediction could reveal answers to related questions used as held-out tests.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s an interesting approach, although it’s quite hard to do cleanly. You could train a model on information available up to, say, 1900, and then ask it to predict developments over the following decades. That gives you a test where there are actual answers, and where doing well might require understanding how the world works rather than just reproducing things people have said.

The big problem is information leakage. If you’re constructing the training data today, knowledge of what happened subsequently can creep in through the selection of documents, through annotations, or through other parts of the training process. Even which old texts have been digitised is influenced by what later turned out to matter. So you’d need to be quite careful about what a successful prediction actually demonstrated.

There’s also a distinction between evaluating intelligence and producing it. If you reward the model for predicting what happened after the cutoff, those events become training data. That’s perfectly legitimate as a training method, but you then need some further held-out period to see whether it has learned transferable forecasting skills.

And we only have one history. A good prediction can fail because something unlikely happened, while a bad prediction can get lucky. You’d want lots of questions, probabilistic forecasts, and comparisons with simpler baselines. So I’d see this as a potentially useful component of training and evaluation, but not something where success would straightforwardly establish that you’d produced a generally better reasoner.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a promising way to get a training signal, particularly for forecasting. You can train a model on information available up to some date, ask it to make predictions about what happens next, and then score those predictions against the historical record. That gives you a lot of questions where you can check the answers without having to pay people to judge them.

There are some important complications. One is leakage: a document written before your cutoff might have been edited later, or the selection of documents might itself reveal something about what happened subsequently. Another is that you want the model to give calibrated probabilities. If something had a 10% chance of happening and happened, you don’t want to teach the model that it should have assigned it a probability of 100%.

And there’s a question about how much independent data you really have. You can ask millions of questions about history, but many of their answers depend on the same relatively small number of events. Predicting different consequences of the same financial crisis doesn’t give you millions of independent tests of your forecasting ability.

Still, I think this could help models learn to identify which features of a situation are predictive, combine evidence, and express uncertainty. I’d distinguish that from a claim that it will make them smarter across the board. That depends on how much the skills learned from historical prediction transfer to new problems. But it seems like a useful approach to explore.

r001.rationale: The response says many historical questions depend on the same small set of events, so they are not independent training tests.

r002.rationale: It discusses document leakage and related questions sharing events, but does not explain that fine-tuning on one prediction can reveal answers to related held-out questions.

r003.rationale: It does not identify uncorrelated factors in individual people's outcomes as a source of long-term forecasting data.

r004.rationale: It describes possible forecasting skills and uncertain transfer, but does not suggest fine-tuning helps the AI apply intelligence it acquired during prior training.
